lead: A living cell is a tiny battery. Its membrane separates charged ions, so the inside sits at a small negative voltage compared with the outside. This resting voltage is near −70 mV. When a stimulus pushes the voltage past a threshold, the cell fires a brief positive spike called an action potential. Every bioelectric recorder — ECG, EEG, EMG — measures these voltages after they have spread through tissue. The cell model explains why the signals exist, why they are small, and why they are brief. This is the electrophysiology behind every recorder.
prereq: You need: school-level idea of a cell membrane and ions, plus the units below; electrode theory is in electrode theory and amplification in bio-amplifiers.

blocks.text: Every cell is wrapped in a lipid membrane. The membrane is a thin insulator. Ion channels are selective pores. The main ions are Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ and large negatively charged proteins. The sodium-potassium pump uses energy from ATP to move three Na⁺ ions out and two K⁺ ions in for each cycle. This pump builds and maintains the concentration gradients: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are high outside; K⁺ and the large negative proteins are high inside.

At rest, K⁺ leak channels are more open than Na⁺ leak channels. K⁺ leaves down its gradient, carrying positive charge out. That makes the inside negative. Na⁺ leaks in and the pump removes it, so the gradients do not run down.

blocks.where: V<sub>m</sub> is membrane voltage; V<sub>inside</sub> is the voltage inside the cell; V<sub>outside</sub> is the voltage outside. A negative V<sub>m</sub> means the inside is negative with respect to the outside.

blocks.text: For one ion, the Nernst equation gives the equilibrium voltage: the membrane voltage at which that ion's concentration push is exactly balanced by the electric pull, so it stops moving on balance.

blocks.where: E<sub>ion</sub> is the equilibrium (Nernst) voltage, inside with respect to outside, in mV; z is the ion's charge (+1 for Na⁺ and K⁺, −1 for Cl⁻); [ion]<sub>out</sub> and [ion]<sub>in</sub> are the concentrations outside and inside in mmol/L. 61.5 mV is 2.303 RT/F at body temperature.

blocks.text: The Goldman equation combines the ions, each weighted by how easily it crosses the membrane (its permeability P). At rest the membrane is most permeable to K⁺, so the resting potential lies close to E<sub>K</sub>; the small Na⁺ leak pulls it a little less negative. In a typical neuron the result is about −70 mV inside. Other cells differ: heart muscle rests near −90 mV.

V<sub>m</sub> = 61.5 mV × log₁₀[(P<sub>K</sub>[K⁺]<sub>out</sub> + P<sub>Na</sub>[Na⁺]<sub>out</sub> + P<sub>Cl</sub>[Cl⁻]<sub>in</sub>) ÷ (P<sub>K</sub>[K⁺]<sub>in</sub> + P<sub>Na</sub>[Na⁺]<sub>in</sub> + P<sub>Cl</sub>[Cl⁻]<sub>out</sub>)]
blocks.where: P<sub>K</sub>, P<sub>Na</sub> and P<sub>Cl</sub> are the relative permeabilities (only their ratio matters). Cl⁻ is negative, so its inside and outside concentrations swap places.

sections.h3: Action potential: threshold, spike and reset

blocks.text: An action potential is a rapid change in V<sub>m</sub> that travels along a nerve or muscle fibre. It starts only when a stimulus depolarises the membrane to threshold. Threshold is a voltage, not a time; a common value is about −55 mV inside. Depolarisation means making V<sub>m</sub> less negative. A stimulus below threshold produces a small local change that dies away. At threshold, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open.

Na⁺ enters, so V<sub>m</sub> rises quickly toward positive values. This is the depolarisation phase. The peak is often near +30 mV. At the peak, Na⁺ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K⁺ channels open. K⁺ leaves the cell, carrying positive charge out, so V<sub>m</sub> falls. This is repolarisation. K⁺ channels close slowly, so V<sub>m</sub> often goes below the resting value. That undershoot is hyperpolarisation. The pump and leak channels then restore the resting state.

After a spike the membrane has a refractory period. During the absolute refractory period no new action potential can start. During the relative refractory period a stronger-than-normal stimulus can start one. The action potential is all-or-none: once threshold is crossed, the height and shape are fixed for that cell. A stronger stimulus does not make a taller spike; it makes more spikes per second. This is why nerve signals carry information in timing and frequency.

A plot of V<sub>m</sub> against time shows rest as a flat line, a sharp rise at threshold, a peak, a fall and a small undershoot. The x-axis is time in milliseconds (ms); 1 ms = 0.001 s. The y-axis is membrane voltage in millivolts (mV); 1 mV = 0.001 V. A typical spike lasts 1–2 ms in a nerve, longer in some muscle cells.

The figure marks rest at −70 mV, threshold at −55 mV, the peak at +30 mV and the undershoot to about −80 mV. Notice that threshold is above rest: it is a depolarised value. The spike amplitude, from rest to peak, is 100 mV; measured from threshold it would be only 85 mV. Recorders do not see the cell directly. An electrode converts ionic current to electronic current (electrode theory), and a bio-amplifier raises the small differential voltage (bio-amplifiers). The ECG, EEG and EMG chapters apply this cell source at body-surface scale.

figure.caption: The worked example's neuron: from rest at −70 mV a stimulus lifts the membrane 15 mV to the −55 mV threshold, Na⁺ inflow drives it to +30 mV, and K⁺ outflow brings it back through a small undershoot. The spike amplitude is 100 mV and the spike lasts about 1.2 ms.

spec.aria: Plot of membrane voltage against time over 5 milliseconds: rest at minus 70 millivolts, threshold at minus 55, a spike to plus 30 and an undershoot to minus 80, with brackets showing 15 millivolts to threshold and a 100 millivolt spike amplitude.

examples.question: A neuron has resting potential −70 mV inside, threshold −55 mV inside, and peak +30 mV inside. (a) Find the depolarisation needed to reach threshold. (b) Find the spike amplitude, from the resting potential to the peak.
steps: Depolarisation to threshold is threshold minus resting voltage: (−55 mV) − (−70 mV) = 15 mV.
Spike amplitude is peak minus resting voltage: (+30 mV) − (−70 mV) = 100 mV.
The two minus signs in each subtraction matter: subtracting a negative voltage adds its magnitude.
examples.answer: The depolarisation needed is 15 mV, and the spike amplitude from rest to peak is 100 mV.
examples.check:
rest = -70
threshold = -55
peak = 30
depolarisation = threshold - rest
amplitude = peak - rest
print(depolarisation)
print(amplitude)

examples.question: A neuron has these concentrations (mmol/L), inside and outside: K⁺ 140 and 5, Na⁺ 15 and 145, Cl⁻ 10 and 110. Take 61.5 mV for 2.303 RT/F at 37 °C. (a) Find the Nernst voltages E<sub>K</sub>, E<sub>Na</sub> and E<sub>Cl</sub>. (b) With relative permeabilities P<sub>K</sub> : P<sub>Na</sub> : P<sub>Cl</sub> = 1 : 0.04 : 0.45, find the resting potential from the Goldman equation.
steps: Goldman numerator (outside K⁺ and Na⁺, inside Cl⁻): 1 × 5 + 0.04 × 145 + 0.45 × 10 = 5 + 5.8 + 4.5 = 15.3.
Goldman denominator (inside K⁺ and Na⁺, outside Cl⁻): 1 × 140 + 0.04 × 15 + 0.45 × 110 = 140 + 0.6 + 49.5 = 190.1.
Check: −67.3 mV lies between E<sub>K</sub> (−89.1 mV) and E<sub>Na</sub> (+60.6 mV) and close to E<sub>K</sub>, because K⁺ has the highest permeability.
examples.answer: E<sub>K</sub> = −89.1 mV, E<sub>Na</sub> = +60.6 mV, E<sub>Cl</sub> = −64.1 mV; the Goldman resting potential is −67.3 mV, close to the usual −70 mV.

traps: Sign slip: resting potential is negative inside; writing +70 mV reverses the cell.
Threshold is a depolarised voltage near −55 mV, not the resting voltage; a stimulus below threshold does not fire.
All-or-none: a stronger stimulus increases firing rate, not spike height.
Unit slip: mV and ms are thousandths; 100 mV = 0.1 V, and 2 ms = 0.002 s.
Spike amplitude is peak minus rest (100 mV here), not peak minus threshold (85 mV). Peak-to-peak runs from the highest to the lowest point, so for this trace it includes the undershoot and is 110 mV.

quiz.q: Define resting potential and state a typical value for a neuron.
quiz.a: Resting potential is the membrane voltage of a cell at rest, inside with respect to outside. A typical neuron value is about −70 mV.

quiz.q: Why is the resting potential negative inside the cell?
quiz.a: K⁺ leak channels let K⁺ leave, carrying positive charge out. The sodium-potassium pump moves three Na⁺ out and two K⁺ in, and Na⁺ leak is small. The result is a negative inside voltage.

quiz.q: A cell has resting potential −70 mV, threshold −50 mV and peak +20 mV. Find the depolarisation to threshold and the spike amplitude from rest to peak.
Why does a stronger stimulus not make a taller action potential?
quiz.a: The action potential is all-or-none. Once threshold is crossed, channel gates and ion gradients set the spike height. A stronger stimulus starts more spikes per second, not a bigger spike.
It is the time after an action potential when a new action potential is hard or impossible to start. Absolute means none can start; relative means a stronger stimulus can start one.

quiz.q: If resting potential is −75 mV and threshold is −60 mV, what depolarisation is needed to reach threshold?
In high blood potassium, [K⁺]<sub>out</sub> rises from 5 to 10 mmol/L with [K⁺]<sub>in</sub> = 140 mmol/L. Find the new E<sub>K</sub> at 37 °C and say what happens to the resting potential.
quiz.a: E<sub>K</sub> = 61.5 × log₁₀(10 ÷ 140) = 61.5 × (−1.146) = −70.5 mV, against −89.1 mV before. The resting potential follows E<sub>K</sub> and becomes less negative, which is why a high potassium level disturbs the heart.

beyond: Not for the exam. Patch-clamp amplifiers record single ion channels, and cardiac and neural drug tests use the same resting and action potential ideas. Wearable biopotential systems push electrodes and amplifiers toward low power and dry contact. Search next for patch clamp, voltage clamp, Hodgkin-Huxley model, and cardiac action potential.
